items.title: Laurence Juber interviewed by Monk Rowe, Glasgow, Scotland, July 27, 2016 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: Aguado, who is pretty much the father of modern classical guitar technique, he was kind of the pedagogue, really the principal pedagogue.

ctx.x: I don’t consider analysis to be the province of classical. We associate music education with classical because we use the classical canon as the core of that repertoire. But because of being a guitar player, and the guitar is not considered truly part of the classical canon, other than the Segovia paradigm, the Spanish classical guitar which Segovia succeeded in bringing the gravitas and putting it in the concert hall. But what he represented in terms of the guitar was a pretty narrow focus. Even within his own…

guitar virtuosi but virtuosi in general outside of that strict classical canon, they were not included. And the level of musicianship that — it is very tangible. That it wasn’t just that they were developing technique. Aguado, who is pretty much the father of modern classical guitar technique, he was kind of the pedagogue, really the principal pedagogue. Fernando Sor, for example, was a very accomplished composer. He was a songwriter, he wrote a vocal method, he wrote a guitar method. He played guitar with really…
method books, they published, they made their money, as much as they could, on publishing. Diabelli published an enormous amount of guitar music.
